findings.summary: The retire rule always flags the steward, audience and auditor, which are in active use, because it never sees their runs.
findings.evidence: compute takes roles only from `records.request_jobs()[..].invocations`. store.rs:239-251 says steward, audience and auditor invocations are "kept apart from `jobs`" in `steward_runs`, `audience_runs` and `auditor_runs`. In the evidence snapshot every steward invocation is a standalone `01-steward.json` with no outcome: 300 files, none at position 02-09. The most recent are 20261111-061048-8bdq and 20261111-055051-pxja. Audience runs also appear repeatedly on Nov 10-11. Request jobs such as 20261110-191311-r241 hold only reader, producer and verifier invocations, plus planner and critic in some jobs. Given more than eight closed jobs, `athena status` will therefore always print "retire candidate: steward/audience/auditor", which is false advice that will appear in every status output. A better rule counts each role's runs in a time window across both the job invocations and the separate run lists, or restricts retirement to roles that run inside jobs. A RoleNeed::compute test over Records with a steward run would catch this.
findings.location: crates/athena-core/src/role_need.rs RoleNeed::compute (ALL_ROLES and the j.invocations scan)

findings.summary: RoleNeed::compute, the actual record reading, has no test.
findings.evidence: All four tests call `analyze` with hand-built NeedJob values. Nothing tests the mapping of outcome states (Failed/Rejected/TimedOut counted as failed; Declined/Closed excluded), the time ordering, or which roles are visible. That gap is why the blocker above went undetected.

findings.summary: The role-needed rule counts each class's whole history with no window, so a class that failed in the past keeps being flagged after it recovers.
findings.evidence: by_class adds up every closed job ever recorded. class_trend, the pattern this module was meant to follow, compares recent windows. A class with many early failures stays a candidate until its successes outnumber them, even after a fix. A recent window, such as the newest N jobs of each class, would follow current need.

findings.evidence: The criterion asks for a StatusView to print the line. The test proves the section formatter works, but not that status() calls it.

summary: The change adds crates/athena-core/src/role_need.rs and wires a `role need` line into `athena status`. It records OLY-9-11's mechanism and measure in docs/spec.toml and adds a CHANGELOG entry. Every changed file is on the deliverables list. I ran the role_need unit tests, the display test and `cargo test -p xtask`, and all pass. CI passed fmt, clippy and the full test suite. All five criteria are met on paper, but the retire rule is wrong on the real records. RoleNeed::compute looks for a role's invocations only inside closed request jobs. store.rs (lines 239-251) says the steward, audience and auditor runs are deliberately kept apart from `jobs`, in `steward_runs`, `audience_runs` and `auditor_runs`. In the evidence snapshot the steward ran 300 times, most recently in 20261111-061048-8bdq, and the audience ran many times on Nov 10-11. None of those runs is inside a request job. So once there are eight closed jobs, which the real records far exceed, `athena status` will always say to retire the steward, audience and auditor, three roles in active use. That makes the measure misleading from the first run, so I judge it a blocker. RoleNeed::compute has no test, which is why nothing caught this. The fix is to also count `records.steward_runs`, `audience_runs` and `auditor_runs`, using their timestamps for the window, or to limit the retire check to roles that run inside jobs. Then add a compute-level test.
